title: A Guide to Listening Well (to Audiobooks)
author: Colton Cauthen
summary: Colton Cauthen, a bookseller who writes the Morning Light newsletter, offers practical advice for readers who want audiobooks to serve a serious reading life rather than replace it. He grants that listening is easier than sitting down with a physical book and then proposes several purposeful uses: as a funnel to decide which books deserve traditional reading time, as a way of prereading a book before a deeper second pass, as a means of meeting obligation reads, as a pairing with a physical book on the same period or author, and as a way to fit in popular novels. He then suggests habits that improve comprehension and retention, such as keeping a physical copy at hand, pausing to discuss the text aloud, and bookmarking key passages. The piece ends with a plug for Libro.fm and a note on free options such as LibriVox and Libby.
points: Audiobooks work best when they have a defined role in a reading plan, whether as a screening funnel, a prereading pass or a way to meet obligation reads.
Pairing an audiobook with a physical book on the same era or author, such as narrative histories alongside Cicero and Virgil, enriches both.
Keeping a physical copy and occasionally checking the table of contents or a chapter opening raises listening comprehension and retention.
Pausing to talk through what you have heard, especially when driving alone, turns passive listening into engagement.
Using the bookmark feature to capture clips and quotes makes it easy to revisit key passages once the book is finished.
quotes: Another way I have used Audiobooks is as a tool for prereading the books that I already knew I wanted to engage with deeply as a physical book. By ‘prereading’ I mean a kind of superficial read where you work through the book to gain an introductory familiarity with its structure, terms content and, in the case of fiction, plot.

To do this, I would take any book I may be interested in reading and begin listening to it, specifically with the intent of determining whether or not it was a book I should put on the more limited list of books I could sit down and read in the near future.
One of my favorite uses for Audiobooks is pairing, which is where I strategically pair an audiobook with a physical book that I am reading.

I have found that occasionally referencing the table of contents and dipping in to read the beginning or end of a chapter here and there increases my “reading” (listening?) comprehension and retention.

A second tip, which works especially well if you are listening while driving alone, is to pause the audiobook occasionally and to discuss it out loud to yourself. Give yourself some time to think about and engage with what you’ve just listened to instead of listening continuously without breaks.

Lastly, I recommend using the bookmark feature found in most audiobook apps, like Libro.fm and Audible to capture important clips, favorite quotes or sections of the book you want to revisit to think more about later.
If you are someone who thinks of reading as a special, formative practice, and would like to get the most out of your audiobooks, this is for you.
